intro.heading: She has the words. She wants him to hear them.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: Mr Hargreaves moved in three weeks ago. His daughter, Helen, lives four hours away and cannot visit every week. She has written a page about his life for the key worker, but she says it is not the same as him hearing her say good morning. She would happily record a short hello and a story about the caravan at Filey. The home has no safe way to take it. She offers to send it to a carer's phone, and the manager is not sure that is wise.

trail.text: Mr Hargreaves moves in. Helen writes up his life story.
The key worker reads it and learns about Filey.
Helen asks, “Could I record him a message?”
There is nowhere safe to send it, so the offer fades.
A carer offers her own phone. The manager says no.
Evenings are hard for him. His daughter's voice sits unrecorded.
Helen asks if the family have done enough. Nobody knows.
“How do you involve his family?” A written page is all you have.

trail_close: The family wanted to give more. The gap is between that kindness and a safe way to use it. Here is how CareStream collects the video, lets you check it, and puts only approved clips in front of staff.

why.heading: A dementia life story is more than a page of facts
why.sub: Voices and faces carry what a document can only describe.

cards.title: A familiar voice settles and connects
cards.body: Life story work with dementia is usually about knowing the person. A short message from a daughter can give staff a way into a conversation, and gives him something to answer.

cards.title: Care should reflect the person
cards.body: Care must meet needs and reflect preferences. Where someone cannot decide for themselves, the Mental Capacity Act asks you to consider their past and present wishes and feelings, and to take into account, where practicable, the views of people interested in their welfare.

cards.title: Video needs a careful gate
cards.body: A clip can show other people, or something the resident would not want played. A manager should watch each one first, and the file should not live on a personal phone. Regulation 10 includes ensuring the privacy of the person.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: A relative wants to send a video for a dementia life story. What do I do?
items.a: You invite them from the resident's record with their name and email, and CareStream emails a private link. On that page they record or choose a short video and add a title. Nothing reaches your team until you have watched it and approved it.

items.q: Does the family need an account or an app?
items.a: No. The link is the way in, with no login and no password. They use the phone they already have. Once they press Send, the link is spent, and if they want to add more later you send a new link.

items.q: How long can a video be?
items.a: Up to 60 seconds, and up to 5 videos on one link, with up to 150MB per upload. If the signal drops the upload carries on from where it stopped. The clip is converted so it plays on a phone, a tablet or a computer, and location details are removed.

items.q: What stops an unsuitable video reaching staff?
items.a: You do. Each family video waits on the Approvals tab. You preview it, edit the title, add a note for staff, and approve or reject it. Rejecting deletes the file at once. Staff only ever see approved videos.
Yes. From the resident's record you can add a video with a title and a note. A video you add is approved at once, because you are the approver.

items.q: Does the system watch the video or describe it?
items.a: No. It never watches or describes a video. It only knows the title, the note and who sent it, so a clear title matters. There are no summaries, no speech to text and no staff downloads.

items.q: What happens if the resident passes away or moves on?
items.a: Their videos leave the hub straight away, and any still waiting are deleted. Approved files stay in private storage for the retention period, like the written profile, then are deleted with it.

items.q: Which plan is it on, and can I try it?
items.a: Resident profiles, photos and videos are on Professional and above. There is a 14 day free trial, and the pricing page shows which plan includes it. You can create an account or book a demo to see it first.

limits.heading: Honest limits: a gathering tool, not a video call

cards.title: It is a message, not a conversation
cards.body: The family record once and the team plays it back. CareStream does not do video calls, and the resident cannot record a reply. If you want a live call, you would arrange that separately.

cards.title: Nothing is automatic
cards.body: A video does not reach staff by itself. A manager has to preview and approve each one, so someone needs to check the Approvals tab. A video nobody approves stays hidden from the team.

cards.title: Titles do the finding
cards.body: The system cannot watch a clip. Staff find it from the title and your note. Videos shown in the hub are the newest ten per resident, and the family cannot see the profile or message you through the link. It is on Professional and above.

faqs.heading: Family video and life story work, answered

items.q: What is a dementia life story?
items.a: It is a record of who the person is: their family, work, places, habits and what matters to them. Staff use it to start conversations and give care that fits. Read more in our guide to the this is me document.

items.q: What is life history work in dementia care?
items.a: Life history dementia work means gathering a person's past, from them and from people who know them, and using it day to day. A short video from a daughter is one way to add her voice to what you already know.

items.q: How does video fit with life story work for dementia?
items.a: Life story work dementia teams do is often written or photographs. Video adds a voice and a face. In CareStream approved videos sit with the resident's profile, so the team can find them when they need them.

items.q: Can the assistant describe what is in a video?
items.a: No. It never watches or describes a video. It only knows the title, the note and who sent it.

items.q: How long can a family video be?
items.a: Up to 60 seconds each, up to 5 on one link, and up to 150MB per upload. The family can add a title of up to 60 characters and remove a clip before pressing Send.

items.q: Does a manager have to approve every video?
items.a: Yes. A family video stays hidden from staff until you approve it. You can edit the title first, or reject it. Videos you add yourself are approved at once.

items.q: Can the family see the videos we approve?
items.a: The link page lets them preview their own clip before they press Send, and after that the link is spent. It does not show the profile or other videos.

items.q: What do the regulations say about involving family?
items.a: Under section 4 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, if it is practicable and appropriate, you take into account the views of anyone interested in the person's welfare. Regulation 9 requires care to reflect people's preferences. Check your own policies on consent and recording.

guide.heading: How to build a dementia life story with family video
guide.lede: A few habits make the difference between a clip that sits unseen and one that helps at four in the afternoon. Ask early, ask for a clear title, and check before you approve.

sections.h3: Ask for a short, warm message
paragraphs: Tell the relative that 30 or 40 seconds is plenty. A hello, the person's name, and one small story is more useful than a long one. Ask them to put a clear title on it, because staff find it by its title.

Watch it as a new carer would, and as the resident might feel about it. Edit the title so it is clear and kind. Reject anything that shows other people who might not want it shared, or anything the resident would find upsetting. You can read what the law says about dignity and respect in regulation 10.
checklist: Is the person speaking someone the resident would be glad to hear?
Does the title say who it is from?
Does it show anyone else who might not want it shared?
Would a new carer know when to use it?

sections.h3: Close the loop with the team and the family
paragraphs: Tell the key worker when a video has been approved and show them where to find it. Thank the relative personally. A dementia awareness course helps staff see why these details matter, and the Mental Capacity Act course covers wishes and best interests.

guide.note: This page describes how the software works and is not legal advice. Check your own policies and local guidance for how you collect and share recordings of residents.
